newsitem.title: USA: U.S. securities firms seek level field with banks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. securities firms seek level field with banks.

text.p: Executives of top Wall Street firms are feeling left out after the Federal Reserve moved Wednesday to lower by several notches some barriers to banking involvement in the securities field.

A frequently-asked question has been why the U.S. Congress has not acted to dismantle depression-era laws and let banks and investment banks into the same financial services arena as practiced in many foreign countries.
One explanation heard on Wall Street is that a rivalry between the banks and the insurance industry got in the way of a legislative solution this year.

When a new Congress reconvenes in 1997 the issue is expected to come up again, but the possiblity of a power shift in the U.S. House of Representatives back to the Democrats could inject some new uncertainties.
Speaking about U.S. investment banks generally, analyst Raphael Soifer of Brown Brothers Harriman said, "a level playing field is still their objective, rather than keeping banks out of their turf."
The analyst continued, "with Congress not having addressed the issue the Fed is going as far as it believes it can under the existing statute."

In its action Wednesday, the Fed permitted banks to share employess between the bank and its securities affiliate; cross-sell products of the securities subsidiary, and buy and sell for its own account a bigger group of securities in transactions with the securities affiliate.

The Federal Reserve is widely expected to list to 25 percent from 10 percent a limit on the amount of underwriting that can be done in a securities affiliate of a bank. The present 10 percent limit is applied to the gross revenues of the securities unit.

In a recent research report, analyst Charles Gabriel of Prudential Securities said banks active in the securities area have been forced to purchase large amounts ot U.S. Treasury issues and carry excess capital in order to inflate the size of their section 20 subsidiaries and reach a critical mass in the investment banking business.

Gabriel said the Fed's actions Wednesday "might improve the economics for smaller banks to engage in these activities." He noted that so far there are only 39 banks with Section 20 subsidiaries and these are mostly the larger banks and units of foreign banks active in the U.S.
